approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that would establish the Housing Australia Future Fund to provide a funding source for social and affordable housing and other acute housing needs.
The package would also create the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council as an independent statutory advisory body to advise the government on housing supply and affordability.

The Housing Australia Future Fund would receive an initial $10 billion credit and aims to fund 30,000 social and affordable homes and allocate $330 million to acute housing needs over its first five years.
Establishes the Housing Australia Future Fund as a funding source for social and affordable housing and acute housing needs.
Creates the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council as an independent advisory body.
Provides an initial $10 billion credit to the Housing Australia Future Fund.
The measures would affect people in need of social and affordable housing, including Indigenous communities, women, children, and veterans.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2023-09-13.72.3) to keep schedule 4 of the [Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr6972%22) unchanged. In parliamentary jargon, they voted that it "stand as printed". Schedule 4 "*contains amendments to Acts that are consequential to the HAFF [Housing Australia Future Fund] Bill and the functioning of the HAFF*" (read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2223a/23bd059) ).
Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023 - Consideration of Senate Message - Agree with Senate amendment

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023 renames the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation (NHFIC) to Housing Australia, extends the Commonwealth guarantee for NHFIC bonds until 30 June 2028, and introduces an annual review mechanism for the National Housing Infrastructure Facility.

The Selection of Bills Committee presented its first report of 2023, referring multiple bills to committees for inquiry, including the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023 and related housing bills to the Economics Legislation Committee with a reporting date of 22 March. Senator McKim moved an unsuccessful amendment to extend that reporting date to 22 April, arguing the government's housing response is inadequate and a longer inquiry is needed to hear from renters and housing sector stakeholders.

The opposition will vote against the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill, arguing it increases inflation and mortgage pressure by relying on $10 billion in borrowed funds with uncertain stock market returns and an estimated $400 million annual interest cost. The opposition will support the other two housing bills except for schedule 4 of the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill.

The opposition argued the Housing Australia Future Fund would increase inflation and interest rates while providing no guaranteed funding for housing projects, costing $400 million annually in interest, and announced they would oppose the bill but support the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council Bill. The Greens argued the fund is inadequate, calling for $5 billion per year in direct investment for social and affordable housing, a two-year rent freeze, and phase-out of negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts, while noting a shortage of 640,000 social and affordable homes and 2.7 million people in rental stress.
